Security definition • The NIST Computer Security Handbook defines computer security as: – The protection afforded to an automated information system in order to attain the applicable objectives of preserving the integrity, availability and confidentiality of information system resources
Computer Security Triad • THREE key objectives are at the heart of computer security – Confidentiality – Integrity – Availability

Additional Concepts • Two further concepts are often added to the core of computer security – Authenticity (genuine; able to be verified and trusted; confidence in the validity of a transmission, message or message originator) – Accountability / Non-repudiation (actions of an entity can be traced uniquely to that entity)

Threats • ISO 27005 defines threat as: – A potential cause of an incident, that may result in harm of systems and organization

Threats • RFC 2828, describes FOUR kinds of threat consequences – Unauthorised Disclosure • Entity gains access to data for which the entity is not authorised – Deception • An event that may result in an authorised entity receiving false data and believing it to be true. – Disruption • An event that interrupts or prevents the correct operation of system of system services and functions. – Usurpation • An event that results in control of system services or functions by an unauthorised entity

Attacks resulting in Unauthorised Disclosure • Unauthorised Disclosure is a threat to confidentiality. • Attacks include: – Exposure (deliberate or through error) • Release of sensitive information such as credit card number, to an outsider. – Interception • On the Internet, a hacker can gain access to email traffic or other data transfers. – Inference • An adversary is able to gain information from observing the pattern of traffic on a network, such as the amount of traffic between particular pairs of hosts on the network. – Intrusion • An adversary gaining unauthorized access to sensitive data by overcoming the system’s access control protections.

Attacks resulting in Deception • Deception is a threat to either system integrity or data integrity. • Attacks include: – Masquerade • An attempt by an unauthorized user to gain access to a system by posing as an authorized user; this could happen if the unauthorized user has learned another user’s logon ID and password. – Falsification • This refers to the altering or replacing of valid data or the introduction of false data into a file or database. For example, a student my alter his or her grades on a school database. – Repudiation • A user either denies sending data or a user denies receiving or possessing the data.

Attacks resulting in Disruption • Disruption is a threat to availability or system integrity. • Attacks include: – Incapacitation • This could occur as a result of physical destruction of or damage to system hardware. • Often malicious software, such as Trojan horses, viruses, or worms, could operate in such a way as to disable a system or some of its services. – Corruption • Malicious software in this context could operate in such a way that system resources or services function in an unintended manner – Obstruction • to interfere with communications by disabling communication links or altering communication control information. • to overload the system by placing excess burden on communication traffic or processing resources.
d the system by placing excess burden on communication traffic or processing resources.

Attacks resulting in usurpation • Usurpation is a threat to system integrity. • Attacks include: – Misappropriation • This can include theft of service. • An example is an a distributed denial of service attack, when malicious software is installed on a number of hosts to be used as platforms to launch traffic at a target host. • In this case, the malicious software makes unauthorized use of processor and operating system resources. – Misuse • Misuse can occur either by means of malicious logic or a hacker that has gained unauthorized access to a system. • In either case, security functions can be disabled or thwarted.
Assets • The assets of a computer system can be categorized as – hardware, – software, – data, – communication lines and networks.

Malware • General term for any Malicious softWare – Software designed to cause damage – Or use up the resources of a target computer. • Some malware is parasitic – Contained within other software • Some malware is self-replicating, others require some other means to propogate.

Backdoor • Trapdoor – Secret entry point • allows someone who is aware of the backdoor to gain access without going through the usual security access procedures. – Useful for programmers debugging • But allows unscrupulous programmers to gain unauthorized access.
Logic Bomb • Explodes when certain conditions are met – Presence or absence of certain files – Particular day of the week – Particular user running application

Trojan Horse • Useful program that contains hidden code that when invoked performs some unwanted or harmful function • Can be used to accomplish functions indirectly that an unauthorized user could not accomplish directly – User may set file permission so everyone has access
Mobile Code • Transmitted from remote system to local system • Executed on local system without the user’s explicit instruction • Common example is cross-site scripting attacks
Multiple-Threat Malware • Multipartite virus infects in multiple ways – Blended attack uses multiple methods – Ex: Nimda has worm, virus, and mobile code characteristics

Parts of Virus • Software that “infects” other software by modifying them • Modification includes – An infection mechanism – Trigger – Payload
Virus Stages • During its lifetime, a typical virus goes through the following four phases: – Dormant phase – Propagation phase – Triggering phase – Execution phase 24
Virus Structure • May be prepended, postpended, or embedded in an executable • When the executable runs, it first executes the virus, then calls the original code of the program

Virus Classification • There is no simple or universally agreed upon classification scheme for viruses, • It is possible to classify a virus by a number of means including – By target – By Concealment strategy
by Target • Boot sector infector • File infector • Macro virus

by Concealment Strategy • Encrypted virus – Random encryption key encrypts remainder of virus • Stealth virus – Hides itself from detection of antivirus software • Polymorphic virus – Mutates with every infection • Metamorphic virus – Mutates with every infection – Rewrites itself completely after every iteration

Macro Viruses • Platform independent – Most infect Microsoft Word documents • Infect documents, not executable portions of code • Easily spread • File system access controls are of limited use in preventing spread 31
E-Mail Viruses • May make use of MS Word macro’s • If someone opens the attachment it – Accesses the local address book and sends copies of itself to contacts – May perform local damage

Worms • Replicates itself • Use network connections to spread form system to system • Email virus has elements of being a worm (self replicating) – But normally requires some intervention to run, so classed as a virus rather than worm 33

Worm Propagation • Electronic mail facility – A worm mails a copy of itself to other systems • Remote execution capability – A worm executes a copy of itself on another system • Remote log-in capability – A worm logs on to a remote system as a user and then uses commands to copy itself from one system to the other

Bots • From Robot – Also called Zombie or drone • Program secretly takes of another Internet attached computer • Launch attacks that are difficult to trace to bot’s creator • Collection of bots is a botnet

Rootkit • Set of programs installed on a system to maintain administrator (or root) access to that system • Hides its existence • Attacker has complete control of the system.
Rootkit classification • Rootkits can be classified based on whether they can survive a reboot and execution mode. – Persistent – Memory based – User mode – Kernel mode
Rootkit installation • Often as a trojan – Commonly attached to pirated software • Installed manually after a hacker has gained root access

Diabetes is a chronic metabolic disorder characterized by elevated blood glucose levels resulting from impaired insulin secretion, insulin action, or both. The disease is associated with severe long-term complications, including cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, diabetic retinopathy, neuropathy, and lower-limb amputations, which significantly affect patients' quality of life and place considerable pressure on healthcare systems. advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) have transformed healthcare by enabling the development of predictive models that support disease diagnosis, prognosis, and clinical decision-making. In diabetes research, machine learning algorithms have been widely applied to analyze patient health records and identify individuals at risk of developing Type 2 diabetes using risk factors such as age, body mass index (BMI), blood glucose level, blood pressure, family history, and lifestyle characteristics. Among the commonly used algorithms are Logistic Regression, Decision Trees, Support Vector Machines, Random Forest, and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), with many studies reporting improved predictive performance compared to conventional statistical approaches. Despite the significant progress achieved in machine learning-based diabetes prediction, several limitations remain evident in existing studies. Most research has primarily focused on improving predictive accuracy by comparing multiple machine learning algorithms, while comparatively little attention has been given to enhancing the interpretability of prediction outcomes and providing users with actionable recommendations that support disease prevention. 12 4 CHAPTER TWO LITERATURE REVIEW 2.1 Introduction Diabetes is a chronic health condition that affects how the body regulates blood glucose levels. It is a major public health concern because uncontrolled diabetes can lead to serious complications, including cardiovascular diseases, kidney damage, nerve damage and vision impairment. Early identification of individuals at risk is important because it creates opportunities for timely health assessment and preventive lifestyle interventions. Traditional approaches to identifying diabetes involve clinical assessments and laboratory tests. Although these methods remain important in healthcare, machine learning has created additional opportunities to analyse health information and identify patterns associated with diabetes (Kavakiotis et al., 2

chine learning has created additional opportunities to analyse health information and identify patterns associated with diabetes (Kavakiotis et al., 2017). Machine learning techniques can examine relationships between medical measurements and recorded health outcomes to generate predictions. Previous studies have investigated different algorithms for diabetes prediction, demonstrating the potential of computational approaches in analysing diabetes-related data (Fregoso-Aparicio et al., 2021; Kavakiotis et al., 2017). However, developing a prediction model is not the only consideration when designing a health-related system. Understanding the factors contributing to predictions and providing useful lifestyle guidance are also important. This chapter reviews literature related to diabetes pr

This chapter reviews literature related to diabetes prediction, the dataset selected for the study, machine learning approaches, data preparation, model evaluation, explainability and recommendation systems. 2.2 Literature Review

13 The Pima Indians Diabetes Database is commonly used in machine learning research involving diabetes classification. The dataset originates from research associated with the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases and the work on using the ADAP learning algorithm to forecast the onset of diabetes mellitus (Smith et al., n.d.). It contains 768 observations from female individuals aged 21 years and above of Pima Indian heritage. The dataset includes eight predictor variables: pregnancies, glucose concentration, blood pressure, skin thickness, insulin level, body mass index, diabetes pedigree function and age. Machine learning is a branch of artificial intelligence that enables computer systems to identify patterns from data and use the learned patterns to make predictions. In supervised learning, models are trained using observations containing input variables and known outcome labels. The models learn relationships between the input variables and the target outcome before their performance is assessed using data that were not used during training. Machine learning and data mining methods have been investigated in diabetes research for classification, prediction and the analysis of diabetes-related in

ne learning and data mining methods have been investigated in diabetes research for classification, prediction and the analysis of diabetes-related information (Kavakiotis et al., 2017). Similarly, Fregoso-Aparicio et al. (2021) reviewed machine learning and deep learning predictive models for Type 2 diabetes, demonstrating the range of computational approaches investigated in this area. The proposed study focuses on Logistic Regression and Random Forest because they provide an opportunity to compare two different supervised classification approaches. Logistic Regression estimates the probability that an observation belongs to a particular class based on its input variables. In diabetes prediction, variables such as glucose concentration, body mass index, age and blood pressure can be used

ass based on its input variables. In diabetes prediction, variables such as glucose concentration, body mass index, age and blood pressure can be used to estimate the probability of a positive outcome. One of its main advantages is its relatively simple structure, which allows its coefficients to be examined to understand how the input variables are associated with the predicted outcome. It can also provide probability estimates rather than only assigning a class label. However, standard Logistic Regression models the relationship between input variables and the log-odds of the outcome as linear.

15 Consequently, complex nonlinear relationships may not be adequately represented without additional transformations or interaction terms. Its performance may also be affected by data quality and relationships between predictor variables. Random Forest, on the other hand, is an ensemble learning algorithm that combines multiple decision trees to produce a classification result. Each tree is trained using a sample of the training data and a random selection of input features, with the individual predictions combined to produce the final result. Unlike standard Logistic Regression, Random Forest can identify nonlinear relationships and interactions between variables without requiring these relationships to be specified manually. This makes it useful for analysing datasets containing differe

tions between variables without requiring these relationships to be specified manually. This makes it useful for analysing datasets containing different clinical measurements. However, because its predictions are generated through multiple decision trees, its behaviour may be more difficult to interpret directly than that of Logistic Regression. Its performance can also depend on the quality of the training data and the selected model parameters. Comparing these two algorithms will therefore help establish which provides more suitable predictive performance on the selected dataset (Kavakiotis et al., 2017). The quality of a machine learning model depends not only on the selected algorithm but also on the quality of the data used during training. Data preprocessing involves examining and pr

odel depends not only on the selected algorithm but also on the quality of the data used during training. Data preprocessing involves examining and preparing raw data to address problems that may affect model performance. (Isnan et al 2024) reviewed preprocessing techniques used in diabetes prediction studies and highlighted the importance of preparing datasets before applying classification algorithms. In the Pima dataset, particular attention is required when investigating missing and invalid values. Some zero values may indicate unavailable measurements, especially in variables where zero is not a realistic clinical measurement. Missing information can be handled through

16 appropriate methods such as removing affected observations or applying statistical imputation, depending on the nature and extent of the missing data. Unusual values also require examination because they may represent either measurement errors or genuine differences between individuals. Techniques such as descriptive statistics, box plots and interquartile range analysis can assist in identifying observations that require further investigation. Removing observations without considering their meaning may result in the loss of useful information. Feature scaling is another preprocessing consideration, particularly when using algorithms that are affected by differences in numerical feature magnitudes. Standardization transforms numerical variables using their mean and standard deviation, w

are affected by differences in numerical feature magnitudes. Standardization transforms numerical variables using their mean and standard deviation, while normalization rescales values to a specified range. Logistic Regression may benefit from feature standardization, particularly when regularization is applied, whereas Random Forest generally does not require scaling because it uses decision-tree splits. The dataset also contains unequal class distributions, with more negative than positive outcomes. This makes it important to examine model performance using more than accuracy alone. Data splitting is equally important because the models should be trained using one portion of the dataset and evaluated using separate observations. Maintaining similar class proportions in the training and t

uld be trained using one portion of the dataset and evaluated using separate observations. Maintaining similar class proportions in the training and testing subsets can support a fairer comparison of model performance. Preprocessing operations should also be fitted using training data before being applied to testing data to reduce the risk of data leakage. Evaluating the performance of diabetes prediction models requires the use of appropriate classification metrics.
